This paper introduces a modified version of the popular Monero cryptocurrency, designed to balance anonymity with transaction efficiency. The proposed system employs lightweight, fast verification for heavy-weight operations by integrating features from both Zcash and I2P. The authors demonstrate the validity of this adaptation through a functional prototype.

This work introduces a novel framework for addressing linear equations within spatial vector spaces, where the solution vector is partitioned into segments, each residing in a distinct Euclidean space. We establish that numerous prominent, yet seemingly unrelated, linear models—including multi-task learning, image restoration, multi-view clustering, and multi-armed bandits—can be unified under this single approach. Furthermore, we develop an innovative, space-toughness-based algorithm for these equations. This method leverages the Nesterov acceleration technique to achieve an optimal convergence rate of $O(\sum_{\ell=1}^L \text{polylog}(T) \cdot (T/\sqrt{t_\ell})^2)$, where $t_\ell$ represents the dimension of the $\ell$-th component space. Additionally, we demonstrate that the proposed space-toughness criterion encompasses and generalizes existing complexity metrics found in the literature for various specific applications.

This study examines the production of three heavy bosons ($W^\pm Z$, $W^\pm \gamma$, or $W^\pm Z\gamma$) in proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. The analysis utilizes data from the CMS experiment, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$, and investigates the kinematic regions where the bosons are highly boosted. Theoretical predictions for the cross-sections are derived using the NNLO+NNLL framework for the $W^\pm Z$ channel and the NLO+NNLL framework for the $W^\pm \gamma$ and $W^\pm Z\gamma$ channels. The study further explores the sensitivity of these processes to the Higgs self-coupling ($\lambda$) and the trilinear gauge-Higgs coupling ($\xi$). The observed data aligns well with theoretical predictions, and the study concludes that the current dataset offers limited sensitivity to the Higgs self-coupling, with a 95% confidence level upper limit of $|\lambda| < 0.35$ relative to the Standard Model value.

We introduce the Hebrew Treebank 2 (HTK2), a new corpus comprising 10,000 annotated sentences of diverse genres, including news articles, fiction, and religious texts. This collection features detailed syntactic labels, semantic roles, and lemmata. To support its utility, we provide a comprehensive set of linguistic statistics and a specialized tokenizer tailored for Hebrew. Additionally, we present a suite of baseline parsers and conduct an in-depth evaluation of their performance.

This work establishes an $\varepsilon$-isometric embedding result where an incompressible subset of $L_p$ (for $1 < p < 2$) into a metric space admitting a coarse $n$-dimensional structure exhibits dimension reduction. Specifically, the embedded subset admits an embedding into a space with coarse $n'$-dimensional structure, where $n'$ is significantly smaller than $n$ relative to the parameter $\varepsilon$.

This paper introduces a new methodology for modeling nonlinear systems by leveraging both system data and existing model knowledge. The core of this approach is a data-informed modeling algorithm that refines a known model by incorporating measured input-output data. This algorithm is built upon the concept of a Wasserstein barycenter, which offers a metric for comparing probability distributions. By utilizing an existing model to define a specific distance metric, the algorithm effectively minimizes the discrepancy between predicted and actual system data. The proposed method is general, applicable to any system with a known model structure, and is demonstrated through a case study involving a nonlinear chemical reactor.

This study examines binary erasure channel (BEC) low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes, specifically analyzing the asymptotic erasure probability as block length approaches infinity. The analysis focuses on a specific class of degree-inhomogeneous graphs where the degree distribution of any node is determined by the degree of its neighboring nodes. The authors derive a set of coupled integral equations to characterize the asymptotic erasure probability for this category. These findings are subsequently applied to specific subgroups, including the degree-dispersed graph family and those possessing a bipartite structure with uniform degree distributions within each side.

This study introduces a novel security filter designed for cyber-physical systems, grounded in the concept of system-level synthesis. The approach involves constructing a finite transition system that encapsulates all feasible trajectories of the underlying cyber-physical model. This system is subsequently encoded into a logical formula, which serves as the basis for developing an automated tool capable of verifying the correctness of the resulting filter.

Decoy-state quantum key exchange (QKD) offers a practical and secure method for distributing keys, yet recent research indicates that adversaries can breach standard decoy-state protocols by exploiting the omission of full phase randomization. This paper investigates such attacks within the context of the practical decoy-state BB84 QKD system and proposes a countermeasure. Simulation results demonstrate that employing our suggested solution effectively nullifies the security risks associated with incomplete phase randomization.

Although in-context learning (ICL) has garnered significant attention, there remains a lack of understanding regarding how pretraining data influences a language model's (LM) ICL capabilities. This study investigates the effects of pretraining datasets on an LM's performance in few-shot tasks, specifically examining the impact of domain alignment and the inclusion of ICL examples within the pretraining corpus. Experiments were conducted across three distinct tasks: natural language inference, machine translation, and question answering. Findings indicate that LMs pretrain on domain-aligned data excel in ICL tasks within that same domain, whereas those pretrain on diverse, domain-agnostic data perform better in out-of-domain scenarios. Furthermore, the research analyzes the consequences of incorporating few-shot training instances into the pretraining dataset, revealing that such inclusion can degrade ICL performance.

We investigate the fragmentation and subsequent expansion of cold clouds within galaxy clusters, a process critical to regulating gas cooling and sustaining the central supermassive black hole. Our numerical simulations model the motion of individual clouds, incorporating physical effects such as radiative cooling, magnetic fields, and thermal conduction. Our findings indicate that while radiative cooling drives cloud fragmentation and expansion, magnetic fields and thermal conduction can either hinder or facilitate this process depending on the specific field geometry. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the fragmentation and growth of these clouds significantly influence their overall survival and dispersal dynamics.

This study examines the CP discrepancy in $B^0 \to K^+ K^-$ decays alongside the $B_s^0 \to K^+ K^-$ system, alongside an analysis of direct CP violation in $D^0 \to K^+ K^-$ decays. Utilizing data from $1.0\,\text{fb}^{-1}$ of $pp$ collisions collected at $\sqrt{s} = 8\,\text{TeV}$ by the LHCb experiment, the measured asymmetry for $B^0 \to K^+ K^-$ is $A_{CP} = -0.062 \pm 0.010 \pm 0.007$. The first uncertainty represents statistical precision, while the second accounts for systematic effects. For the $B_s^0 \to K^+ K^-$ channel, the measured asymmetry is $A_{CP} = -0.003 \pm 0.011 \pm 0.006$, where the uncertainties are similarly categorized as statistical and systematic. The analysis further investigates the dependence of these asymmetries on the invariant mass of the final-state kaon pair. Finally, the results are contrasted with theoretical predictions.

We introduce novel four-point scattering amplitudes for the open superstring theory, which encompass an extended version of the critical bosonic open string amplitude. By applying the extended Gross conjecture, we derive closed-form expressions for our proposed superstring amplitudes.

The advent of 5G cellular networks introduces new challenges in central management, driven by the escalating demand for network resources and the growing intricacy of network architecture. To address these hurdles, this paper outlines the fundamental central management processes required for 5G systems, with a specific focus on self-optimization, self-configuration, and self-healing capabilities. Additionally, the work examines the interplay between these central management functions and the network's self-sustaining attributes.

This study introduces a novel approach to resource-free speech synthesis by utilizing transcripts composed of perceptual auditory units. We trained a neural network to generate these unit sequences from audio, leveraging the fact that they align more closely with human hearing than traditional acoustic units. Subsequently, we developed a zero-resource text-to-auditory-unit conversion model to support a neural speech synthesis system. This framework was evaluated on the challenging task of creating synthetic voices for the VoxPopuli dataset, achieving a top-3 ranking in the associated 2020 challenge.

This study addresses motion planning as a multi-stage convex programming challenge, where each phase involves determining a trajectory segment between two specific waypoints. To enhance computational efficiency, we introduce a data-driven methodology for tightening the solution space by leveraging the data-specific properties of the system's dynamics. Specifically, we develop a data-guided algorithm to construct refined McCormier envelope relaxations of the dynamic models, which subsequently accelerate the resolution of each sub-problem. The proposed approach is validated through simulations involving a quadcopter quadrotor executing maneuvers within a cluttered environment.

This work investigates the constraints on transforming one quantum state into another under the requirement that the process must succeed with a specific probability. We demonstrate that, unlike transformations that succeed with certainty, those with non-certain success rates are subject to strict additional restrictions. Specifically, we prove that such probabilistic transformations mandate the existence of an eigenvalue gap within the target state. These findings are further generalized to encompass multiple-to-many transformations.

This study examines the sloshing dynamics of a viscous fluid within a cylindrical container undergoing horizontal pendulum motion, with a focus on developing a mechanism to replicate coffee shop coffee sloshing. The research utilizes a two-dimensional, depth-averaged model that incorporates viscous effects and demonstrates that the fluid's behavior is governed by the Reynolds number, the Atwood number, and the P\'eclet number. The paper presents both experimental results and numerical simulations, which are compared to show strong agreement with theoretical predictions.

Decentralized learning aims to train a shared model across multiple devices, where each device holds a distinct data distribution. This setup, often referred to as heterogeneous learning, introduces significant challenges due to the heterogeneity of data. To address this, we introduce DR-DSGD, a novel teaching algorithm designed for heterogeneous learning environments. DR-DSGD integrates Duality Theory with Wasserstein Robust Optimization to mitigate the adverse effects of data heterogeneity. Specifically, the algorithm employs a dual-based reformulation of the Wasserstein robust loss function, enabling the computation of model updates at each device. These local updates are informed by dual variables representing probability distributions of data loss, which are subsequently aggregated via a gossip protocol. The dual variables themselves are refined through a distributed subgradient approach. We provide theoretical analysis demonstrating that DR-DSGD converges to a stationary point of the original robust optimization problem. Additionally, we offer a convergence bound for the algorithm and empirically validate its performance through simulations.

We investigate the impact of hydrodynamic pullers on particle production within relativistic heavy-ion collisions. Our findings indicate that even a modest concentration of these agents significantly alters the initial energy density and temperature, leading to markedly different outcomes regarding particle generation. Specifically, the presence of pullers reduces the final multiplicity of produced particles. This suppression occurs because the pullers exert a negative work on the fluid, thereby lowering the initial energy density and diminishing the fluid's expansion velocity. Consequently, the system's cooling rate accelerates, resulting in a shorter duration of the phase transition. We further demonstrate that the multiplicity of generated particles scales inversely with the count of pullers, a relationship that can be utilized to constrain the properties of these objects.

The origins of protostellar outflows remain a subject of debate. This study investigates the outflow properties of the high-velocity jet-driven system IRAS 16293-2422 by analyzing its spectral energy distribution (SED) and submillimeter continuum data. Our findings indicate that the system's jet originates from a protostar with a mass of approximately 0.15 solar masses, embedded within a dense envelope weighing roughly 1.5 solar masses. The protostar is located at a distance of about 100 astronomical units from the envelope's center. Additionally, the system exhibits a low-velocity outflow with a mass-loss rate of roughly $10^{-6}$ solar masses per year. These results suggest that high-velocity jets from forming stars can generate low-velocity outflows, a mechanism that may explain the coexistence of both flow types observed in many young stellar objects.

This study introduces a novel control framework for constrained nonlinear systems, designed to balance system performance with adherence to constraints. The proposed method relies on an equilibrated regulation strategy, where the controller dynamically adjusts between a performance-oriented mode and constraint-enforcement mode based on the current state. This switching behavior is managed by a hysteresis mechanism to ensure smooth transitions. The analysis demonstrates that the closed-loop system maintains ultimate boundedness, with the equilibrium point residing within a specific constraint region. Furthermore, the paper presents a hybrid control approach for systems featuring both state and input constraints, ensuring feasibility and guaranteeing stability.

This study examines the resonant behaviors arising from solar radiation pressure within the circular restricted three-body framework. We develop an analytical approximation for the force vector generated by solar radiation pressure and utilize it to construct closed-form expressions for the resonant locations of both the direct and reverse semi-secular resonances. Furthermore, we introduce numerical techniques to derive precise approximations for these same resonances. The validity of our proposed analytical method is confirmed through comparisons with these numerical results.

We introduce a first-principles methodology for constructing tight-binding models that accurately represent light-matter interactions, specifically designed to capture the quantum nature of the electromagnetic field. By applying the frozen photon technique, we derive tight-binding parameters for the photonic component, utilizing an approach analogous to the frozen-atom method employed for electrons. This framework enables the explicit calculation of optically induced modifications to matter systems, such as changes in electronic band structures and the creation of artificial gauge fields. Furthermore, we demonstrate the measure-invariant stability of key phenomena, including topological states and photon band structures, across varying gauge choices.

This study introduces a novel category-level perception framework designed to estimate object pose and shape using semantic keypoints from 2D images and 3D point clouds. Unlike traditional methods that rely on instance-specific training data, this approach learns object representations from semantic keypoints, enabling robust pose and shape estimation for new object categories. To achieve this, the authors propose a new architecture called the Ideal Pose and Shape Estimator (IPSE). IPSE consists of two primary components: a shape estimator that predicts an object's canonical shape from semantic keypoints, and a pose estimator that aligns the predicted shape to the target object's pose. Furthermore, the paper presents a resilience module that refines shape predictions by integrating both 2D and 3D semantic information. Experiments conducted on the ShapeNet dataset demonstrate that this keypoint-based method surpasses existing state-of-the-art instance-specific techniques.

This study introduces a novel method for constructing confidence intervals for the location and scale parameters of a Cauchy distribution, based on the maximum likelihood estimators. The proposed intervals utilize the asymptotic distribution of these estimators, specifically the non-central t-distribution, to achieve the desired coverage probability. Simulation results are presented to compare the performance of this approach with existing methods.

Basket trials are increasingly utilized in medical research to evaluate multiple drug indications simultaneously, allowing for the rapid assessment of various conditions. A primary objective in these trials is to identify the optimal dose level for each specific indication. This study introduces a Bayesian framework for dose-finding basket trials that permits borrowing information across subsets. The methodology employs a continuous borrowing parameter, which is estimated alongside the dose-finding metrics to dynamically adjust the extent of information sharing. This approach is applicable to both scenarios where the dose is uniform across all indications and where distinct doses are selected per indication. The proposed method was validated through simulation analyses, and its practical utility was demonstrated using a simulated case study.

This paper introduces a novel sequence-based multi-loop control strategy designed for high-precision motion systems, utilizing a linear parameter-varying (LPV) framework. The proposed approach extends the concept of sequential loop shutting (SLS), originally developed for single-loop control, to a multi-loop context. The control architecture consists of a series of distinct single-loop configurations, each targeting a specific system dynamic. By leveraging a polytopic LPV model, the various controller sets are smoothly blended. The resulting control scheme offers significant advantages, including reduced complexity, diminished order requirements, and enhanced performance. The efficacy of this method is demonstrated through simulations involving a motion system tasked with tracking complex trajectories.

This study introduces PRNet, a novel deep learning framework designed for aligning two arbitrary 3D point clouds. Unlike previous methods that rely on global aggregation to estimate transformation parameters, PRNet utilizes local neighborhood information to derive these features. This shift allows the system to handle partial objects with missing data and enhances robustness against noise. Furthermore, the method employs self-supervised learning to generate training labels, eliminating the need for explicit point-to-point correspondences. Extensive testing on both synthetic data and real-world scans confirms that the approach achieves superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques.

We investigate the $R_\infty$ property for generalized solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups, determining the exact $R_\infty$ characteristic for all such groups that admit a nilpotent quotient. Additionally, we establish sufficient conditions under which these groups possess the $R_\infty$ property.

The Standard Model permits a metastable vacuum, a state that could theoretically decay into a lower-energy configuration. This paper examines the collider requirements necessary to confirm such vacuum decay. We introduce a universal framework that defines the necessary conditions for establishing this phenomenon, regardless of the specific experimental setup. Applying this model, we analyze various colliders and determine that a 100 TeV proton-proton collider is required to confirm the instability, given current constraints on the Higgs mass and top quark mass.

This study introduces a robust optimization-based method for reconstructing time-varying sources from measurements of their forward evolution. The approach is formulated within a trajectory framework, where the source is modeled as a continuous path in a function space. By employing a specific optimization criterion, the method simultaneously determines the entire temporal source profile. Numerical simulations demonstrate that the technique effectively recovers piecewise-constant and discontinuous time-dependent inputs, even in the presence of noisy data.

This study employs the Bethe-Salpeter wave function to determine the $D^*$ and $D^*_s$ meson allocation amplitudes. The results indicate that the $D^*$ and $K^*$ mesons share nearly identical amplitudes, whereas the $D^*_s$ meson exhibits a significantly reduced value. These findings are consistent with the predictions of the quark model.

This work establishes the Fourier-based characterization of Gelfand-Shilov spaces $S_{1,\delta}^b$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$ for parameters $0<\delta\leq1$ and $b\in\mathbb{R}$, utilizing Paley-Wiener type theorems for specific subspaces of tempered distributions. We further demonstrate the non-triviality of these spaces when $\delta<1$ through the use of smooth bump functions. Additionally, we derive novel smoothness criteria for the Gelfand-Shilov semigroup $G_\delta^t$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$ for $0<\delta\leq1$ and $t>0$, which finds direct application in characterizing the domains of fractional powers of the Laplacian and analyzing Toeplitz operators defined on the Fock space $F_\delta^2$.

Unlabeled data is frequently employed to enhance the performance of domain adaptation and cross-modal retrieval systems. However, a significant challenge remains: instances within this unlabeled set are often mixed across various modalities, making it difficult to determine their specific category. This paper introduces a novel approach to resolve this issue by partitioning instances into distinct modalities. We propose a Cyclic Partitioning Generative Adversarial Network (CP-GAN) that leverages the cyclic consistency inherent in unlabeled data to generate modality-specific labels. Experiments conducted on three datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms existing techniques.

This study introduces a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) designed for human action prediction, which incorporates a Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernel-based feature mapping layer. This addition aims to enhance the model's capacity to capture intricate temporal dependencies within action sequences. Empirical evaluations on two distinct action prediction benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques.

The 1985 April 12 Great Eruption of the symbiotic star AD Leo was the most significant event recorded for this system. This study presents the first comprehensive spectral analysis of AD Leo during the peak of that eruption, utilizing 19 near-ultraviolet (NUV) spectra obtained from the Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph (STIS) on the Hubble Space Telescope. The observed NUV spectra reveal a broad emission feature centered at approximately 2000 Å, which we attribute to the combined effects of the Lyman-alpha line and the Balmer gamma line. Additionally, numerous narrow emission lines are detected, primarily corresponding to the Balmer series and the Mg II doublet. We constructed a model spectrum by combining the spectra of a K-type giant star with those of a hot, dense wind, aiming to replicate the observed features. Our results indicate that the NUV spectrum of AD Leo during the 1985 eruption is dominated by the emission from the hot wind component.

We examine the deformation theory of $\mathrm{G}_2$-instantons within nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$-holonomy structures, demonstrating that these instantons correspond to critical points of a specific functional defined over the space of such geometries. Furthermore, we establish a one-to-one mapping between the infinitesimal deformations of $\mathrm{G}_2$-instantons (keeping the underlying structure fixed) and those of the nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$-holonomy itself (keeping the instanton fixed).

This paper investigates $C$-normal weighted composition operators acting on the space of square-integrable Hardy functions, $H^2$. We establish sufficient conditions under which these operators are normal and derive the specific forms of linear differential equations they satisfy. Additionally, we determine the exact structure of the underlying composition and weighting pairs.

We introduce a novel combinatorial method to determine the $p$-core $p'$-degree of the symmetric group $S_n$. This approach relies on a specific mapping from the set of all $p$-partitions of $n$ to the partitions of $n-p$. We define this map as the big $p$-core $p'$-configuration, which functions as a weighted, directed graph. Within this structure, the $p$-core $p'$-degree of $S_n$ corresponds to the average out-degree of its nodes. Furthermore, we establish a combinatorial formula for the $p$-core $p'$-degree of a particular class of partitions, the $p$-regular staircase partitions.

Point cloud deep learning models have achieved significant success across various applications, yet their performance is often hindered by the inherent ambiguity of point representations, which causes inconsistent learning outcomes. Existing methods attempt to mitigate this instability by employing data augmentation strategies such as random dropping or rotating, but these approaches fail to address the core issue effectively. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Transformation-Unique Point Cloud (TPC), a novel smoothing framework designed to enhance model robustness against point cloud irregularities. The proposed method constructs a Unique Point Cloud (UPC) for each input, where the point order is determined by the intrinsic geometric structure. Subsequently, the system applies data smoothing by randomly permuting points within these unique structures during training. This strategy not only reduces representation instability but also leverages the inherent geometric properties to generate more meaningful augmented samples. Extensive experiments across multiple applications demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques.

This paper introduces and evaluates two methods for enabling FMCW radars to operate within a shared network: slotted ALOHA and CSMA. The slotted ALOHA approach is implemented via a central coordinator that distributes time slots for chirp transmission, while the CSMA method allows radars to sense the presence of other devices' chirps and defer their own transmission accordingly. Both protocols were tested using a prototype system built from commercial off-the-shelf components, and the results demonstrate that the CSMA implementation achieves superior performance compared to the slotted ALOHA approach.

We introduce a theoretical framework for investigating Entangled two-photon Absorption (TPA) within Hong-Ou-Mandel (HOM) interference setups. In this model, a TPA event occurs when a single molecule absorbs an entangled photon pair, resulting in the molecule's excitation to a doubly excited state. Our analysis reveals that TPA generates spectral reflections corresponding to the characteristic two-photon interference patterns. Specifically, we demonstrate that the absorption spectrum exhibits two distinct peaks, with the central region displaying a dip. This dip signifies the suppression of the Hong-Ou-Mandel effect driven by TPA. Additionally, we explore the sensitivity of this phenomenon to variations in the polarization states of the incident entangled photons.

This paper calculates the circle-equivariant elliptic cohomology of the complex projective space CP(V), where V represents a complex vector space equipped with a linear circle-equivariant circular structure.

Predicting future facts in temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs) is a challenging task that requires handling both knowledge gaps and time-varying entity relations. While representation learning has emerged as a leading approach for TKG inference, existing models often struggle with scalability and overfitting. This study introduces a model-agnostic, low-rank representation framework designed to enhance current inference capabilities. By decomposing entity and relation embeddings into shared and unique subspaces, the proposed method effectively captures both common and distinctive characteristics of head and tail entities across different temporal contexts. Furthermore, the framework extends established static and dynamic TKG representations to ensure compatibility with various architectures. Empirical evaluations on standard benchmarks demonstrate that this approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving substantial improvements in both link prediction and entity linking tasks.

This paper examines how ground noise influences the performance of a single-antenna ground-based receiver targeting a high-speed, low-altitude satellite. The study analyzes two distinct ground models: one representing a flat surface with random roughness and another simulating a complex urban environment. For the flat ground scenario, the authors employ the Small-Slope Approximation (SSA) method to derive the autocorrelation function of the noise, subsequently calculating key metrics such as the mean, variance, and skewness of the received signal. In the urban context, the authors utilize the 3GPP 3-D ray-tracing tool to generate noise samples, from which they compute the same statistical parameters. Finally, the work evaluates the impact of ground noise on the bit error rate (BER) for both Binary Phase-Shift Keying (BPSK) and Quadrature Phase-Shift Keying (QPSK) modulation schemes.

This study demonstrates a perfect illustration of quantum nonlocality without inequalities, utilizing non-perfect correlations within the standard CHSH framework. We establish that violating the Bell criterion for entangled states without applying any inequality holds true even when the maximal violation of the CHSH inequality is not achieved. Furthermore, we prove that for every entangled state, a suitable measurement configuration allows for the flawless demonstration of this specific type of Bell nonlocality.

This work examines the impact of disorder on the Hofstadter model featuring random potentials, specifically focusing on the regime of weak quasi-periodic disorder. We demonstrate that, regardless of disorder strength, energy bands split into numerous sub-bands characterized by narrow energy gaps. Furthermore, we show that the widths of these narrow gaps scale exponentially with system size, a phenomenon indicative of localized states within each level band. Additionally, we find that the mobility edges separating localized and extended states coincide with band edges in the clean system. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the interpretation of prior numerical studies.

The hydrogen-rich hydride materials, which exhibit high-pressure superconductivity, have sparked significant interest as potential candidates for room-temperature superconductivity. Among these, hydrogen boride (LiBH4) is a hydrogen-dense compound that has not yet been thoroughly investigated regarding its superconducting properties. In this study, we employ first-principles calculations to analyze the structural, electronic, and vibrational characteristics of LiBH4. Our results indicate that LiBH4 possesses a stable hexagonal structure at 100 GPa, featuring a high hydrogen content of 12.5 wt% and a wide electronic band gap. Furthermore, we computed the phonon dispersion relations and the electron-phonon coupling matrix elements for the hexagonal phase. The calculated electron-phonon interaction strength is marginal, resulting in a predicted critical superconducting transition temperature ($T_c$) of only 1.5 K. Consequently, our findings suggest that hydrogen boride is unlikely to be a promising high-temperature superconductor.

This study introduces a novel approach to partitioning and distributing workloads across a cluster by flattening the traditional multi-dimensional task assignment space into one dimension. This shift enables the use of established, efficient 1-dimensional algorithms for task allocation. To support this framework, we present a new data structure called the Flattened Range Sum Query (FRSQ), which allows for rapid computation of task metrics such as memory usage, CPU cycles, and network traffic. We further detail an algorithm for constructing and maintaining the FRSQ with logarithmic time complexity for both updates and queries. Empirical evaluations on real-world datasets demonstrate that this method achieves performance comparable to existing state-ofthe-art techniques while significantly reducing computational overhead.

We establish the $l$-charmability and $l$-rigidity of arithmetic $l$-compact groups for all primes $l$. Additionally, we prove the $l$-charmability and $l$-(quasi-)rigidity of $l$-compact topological full groups associated with minimal, uniquely ergodic, and essentially free actions of arithmetic $l$-compact groups.

This paper introduces a fail-functional driving system for vehicles, validated through formal methods. The system operates by utilizing two independent driving modules that alternate control, with a failure detector identifying malfunctions to switch off the defective module and activate the healthy one. This architecture ensures continuous driving capability even after a single fault. The work formally defines the system's behavior and verifies key properties, including the absence of deadlocks, the guaranteed execution of control logic, and the correctness of the fail-operational mechanism. These conclusions are supported by models developed in the OCaml programming language and verified using the Coq proof assistant.

This paper introduces a novel data-driven approach for clustering dynamical systems, which operates by calculating a specific influence metric between data points. This metric is derived from the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) and is defined within a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKH S) utilizing a kernel function that models the underlying system dynamics. The influence measure subsequently guides the clustering process through the adaptation of a standard Mixture Model Clustering (MM C) algorithm. The efficacy of this proposed method is validated via simulations on both linear and linear systems.

This paper examines the techniques of Leibniz's differential and integral calculus, which rely on the concept of variable quantities capable of fluctuating across multiple values. We analyze Leibniz's methods within three modern frameworks: the hyperreal numbers, smooth nonstandard analysis, and the theory of finitists.

Intensity mapping offers a method to measure the 21 cm radiation from neutral hydrogen (HI) across vast cosmic volumes, with interferometric intensity mapping (IM) specifically targeting the spatial fluctuations of the HI brightness temperature. Disturbances in the observed signal arise from the target cosmological signal combined with various foreground contaminants. This study investigates how these foregrounds influence the observed power spectrum of the IM signal. We demonstrate that, in the absence of calibration errors, IM foregrounds do not generate spurious power; however, they can suppress the cosmological signal through background subtraction techniques. We derive an analytical model for this suppression and validate it against numerical simulations. Our findings indicate that the magnitude of this suppression is contingent upon the specific foreground spectral model employed. Consequently, the proposed analytical framework provides a valuable tool for forecasting the sensitivity of future IM experiments.

It establishes the existence of unital $C^*$-algebras where the dimensionality cannot be deduced from any other $C^*$-algebra, even without constraints, by utilizing specific ideals. Although hybrid recommender systems have proven effective in addressing the limitations inherent in individual collaborative and content-based methods, they often neglect the contextual information found within documents. This study introduces a novel, context-aware hybrid framework that integrates both document context and user behavior to boost recommendation quality. The proposed system utilizes two distinct components: a document-contextual approach that leverages topic modeling to generate context-sensitive suggestions, and a behavior-oriented approach that employs matrix factorization to capture user-item interactions. Evaluated against three public datasets, the results demonstrate that this new framework significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art hybrid models.

This paper investigates random matrices exhibiting freeness of type $B$ alongside conditional independence, with a specific focus on deriving conditional moment bounds and characterizing conditional free Poisson distributions.

This paper re-examines the observation of timed characteristics within the framework of timed automata. We demonstrate that the set of all possible observations forms a recognizable subset of infinite words, a result that generalizes the findings of Alur and Henzinger (1993). Furthermore, we show that observations for certain extended variants of these systems also remain regular. This approach yields an alternative derivation of the decidability of the controllability problem for timed games, a result originally established by Bouyer et al. (2001).

The decay process $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi \pi^0 \eta$ is investigated using an effective field model that incorporates both $s$-wave and $p$-wave contributions. The study reveals that the $s$-wave component is driven by the blending of $f_0(980)$ and $a_0(980)$ resonances, whereas the $p$-wave arises from the $K\bar K^*$ system. The predicted branching fraction is $1.1^{+0.4}_{-0.3}(\text{stat})^{+0.3}_{-0.2}(\text{syst})\times 10^{-5}$, a value consistent with the recent measurement from the LHCb collaboration.

The GRAVITY instrument, a next-generation version of the VLTI/Interferometer, is designed to harness the capabilities of the Very Large Telescope Interferometer alongside its four Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI) Auxiliary Telescopes (VLT). It employs a four-beam beam combiner system that integrates the light from the VLTI's four interferometers, enabling the observation of astronomical sources with an effective baseline extending up to 200 meters. This instrument achieves an angular resolution of approximately 0.4 milliarcseconds and a spectral precision reaching 10^-6. The core of the system is the GRAVITY Beam Combiner, which utilizes four beam combiners to merge signals from the VLTI's four interferometers, allowing observations with an effective baseline of up to 200 meters. The core of the system is the GRAVITY Beam Combiner, which utilizes four beam combiners to merge signals from the VLTI's four interferometers, allowing observations with an effective baseline of up to 200 meters. The instrument achieves an angular resolution of approximately 0.4 milliarcseconds and a spectral precision reaching 10^-6. The core of the system is the GRAVITY Beam Combiner, which utilizes four beam combiners to merge signals from the VLTI's four interferometers,

This work examines the computational characteristics of the $k$-center problem within metric spaces defined by a directed graph $G=(V,E)$ and edge weights $w$. In this generalized setting, the distance between any two nodes $u$ and $v$ corresponds to the minimum cost of a path from $u$ to $v$. The objective is to select a subset of $k$ vertices such that the maximum distance between any pair of selected centers and all other nodes is minimized. We introduce a new metric dimension termed the "freeway dimension," which serves as the natural extension of the concept used for undirected graphs. Our findings demonstrate that this problem is approximable within a factor of $\tilde{O}(d_{\text{fw}})$, where $d_{\text{fw}}$ represents the freeway dimension. Furthermore, we prove that the freedom dimension acts as the optimal parameter for approximation by establishing its hardness for achieving a better factor. These results also imply that the freedom dimension is the correct generalization of the doubling dimension found in Euclidean space. Finally, we show that the freedom dimension can be significantly larger than the standard treewidth, distinguishing it clearly in graph theory applications.

This study investigates the relationship between an entire function and its exponential shift, specifically focusing on how the Lebesgue measure of the difference set $E-\Delta$ relates to the order of $E$. Additionally, we examine the uniqueness of the function $E$ by considering the five-value set $E\cup\Delta$ and the five-omitted set $E\cup\Delta$.

This study addresses the task of solving systems of linear equations over finite fields, where each query to the equation system may return an incorrect result with a probability bounded by $\delta < 1/2$. The authors establish new lower bounds for this problem and introduce a novel method termed "early stopping." This technique enables the solver to determine the equation system's solution using fewer queries than previously established upper limits allowed.

We introduce a novel symmetry-protected topological (SPT) phase characterized by parity-guaranteed corner emission. This phase arises in a square lattice with $C_4$ rotational symmetry, where the system's Hamiltonian is constructed using a parity-symmetric Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) model defined on a moiré lattice. Although the system is gapped and lacks intrinsic zero-energy modes in the bulk or at the edges, corner states are topologically secured by the combination of $C_4$ symmetry and particle-hole symmetry. Specifically, the eight corners of a finite system host four pairs of zero-energy modes, with their positions and existence determined by the bulk parity eigenvalues under $C_4$. Furthermore, these corner modes exhibit chiral dynamics governed by an effective non-Abelian gauge field, a phenomenon that can be probed experimentally using ultracold atoms.

This study introduces a rigorous analytical framework for the thermodynamics of an equilibrium alkali plasma, a system defined by the coexistence of three distinct particle species: neutral atoms, positive ions, and electrons. The derived analytical expressions for thermodynamic potentials are expressed in terms of the Saha ionization degree, a parameter that quantifies the ratio of ions to neutral atoms. The paper presents explicit, closed-form formulas for the internal energy, pressure, and entropy, alongside a precise calculation of the ionization degree itself. The validity of these theoretical results is confirmed through comparison with numerical simulations.

This study examines the vector meson spectrum within a medium exhibiting chiral asymmetry, which arises from the vacuum of fermions. We employ the Bethe-Salpeter equation alongside the dynamical model of chiral quarks to determine the mass spectrum. Our findings reveal that vector mesons acquire a dependence on chiral chemical potential, which modifies their masses. Additionally, we observe that the medium induces a splitting of vector meson masses based on their spin projection along the direction of the chiral chemical potential.

This paper addresses the task of estimating key network properties, such as average degree and diameter, from a single snapshot of a graph. We focus on a distributed model where nodes operate as Byzantine agents capable of sending arbitrary, inconsistent messages to one another. Our proposed algorithms achieve an accurate estimation of these metrics using only a sublinear number of communication steps, provided the graph adheres to the small-world property.

Numerical relativity simulations of binary black hole mergers typically rely on the Bowen-York method to generate initial data, which imposes specific constraints on black hole spin and separation. This paper introduces a new algorithm that overcomes these restrictions, allowing for the construction of initial data involving arbitrary masses and spins with adjustable separation. The method employs a conformal decomposition where the extrinsic curvature is modeled as a sum of analytically known multipole terms and an unknown conformal remainder. By applying a spectral method to the resulting Hamiltonian constraint, the algorithm solves for the remainder and the conformal factor iteratively. Validation against test problems confirms the approach's accuracy, and initial data sets created using this technique have been utilized in binary black hole merger simulations.

The upcoming Large Water Cherenkov neutrino Observatory (LWO), or JUNO, aims to investigate neutrino oscillations and detect low-energy neutrinos from nuclear reactors. A key component of this project involves employing approximately 5,000 20-inch photomultiplier tubes (PMTs) to identify Cherenkov light within the water volume. To ensure the instrument's performance, these PMTs must be rigorously screened for dark count rates and photon detection efficiency, with a specific focus on evaluating their light yield across different wavelengths. This study details the assessment of 20-inch PMTs using a newly developed, large-area, and wide-spectral-response optical test setup.

Graph neural networks (GNNs) have proven highly effective for forecasting multidimensional time series by modeling dependencies between variables through a graph structure. However, existing approaches often rely on fixed, static graphs that fail to account for potential shifts in these relationships over time. This study introduces a novel adaptive GNN framework designed to learn GNN architectures directly from data. The proposed method utilizes a meta-learning strategy to optimize graph structures for forecasting tasks, employing a specialized self-attention mechanism to derive the graph's adjacency matrix. Experiments conducted on both synthetic datasets and real-world multivariate time series demonstrate that this approach surpasses current state-of-the-art methods.

This study introduces a suite of atmospheric models designed to simulate the light curves of transiting exoplanets, with a specific focus on those exhibiting low signal-to-noise ratios. The primary objective is to investigate how various physical parameters influence the resulting light curves. The paper details the development of these models and analyzes their sensitivity to key variables, including the planet's radius, equilibrium temperature, and the atmospheric scale height. The work concludes by outlining the models' applications for characterizing atmospheric signals in exoplanetary transit events.

Knowledge distillation (KD) is a method where a compact "student" model learns from a consortium of larger "teacher" models. While prior research has primarily focused on single-teacher setups, recent advancements have expanded to multi-teacher paradigms. However, these approaches often suffer from inconsistent teacher outputs and a lack of cohesive learning signals. To address these issues, we introduce Pairwise Iterative Logits Aggregation (PILE), an innovative multi-teacher framework. PILE iteratively refines teacher predictions by aggregating logits in pairs, thereby enhancing output consistency. Furthermore, it employs a collaborative learning strategy that enables teachers to benefit from one another, sharpening their own outputs through mutual interaction. Extensive experiments across various domains—including speech recognition, image classification, and machine translation—demonstrate that PILE significantly boosts distillation performance.

We introduce a novel detection strategy for ultralight dark matter (DM) utilizing a dual-spinning, dual-frequency, dual-beam interferometer. This approach capitalizes on the oscillatory oscillations induced by DM fields, which generate oscillating forces on a test mass. By precisely measuring the test mass's response to these stimuli, the system can identify ultralight DM candidates. The study demonstrates that this technique offers superior sensitivity for detecting ultralight DM compared to existing methods, specifically for masses ranging from $10^{-13}$ to $10^{-10}$ eV.

This study examines the uniqueness of solutions for basis pursuit within the continuum. We establish sufficient conditions for unique resolvability, categorized into two contexts: the discrete case and the case of piecewise constant functions. In the discrete setting, we derive criteria based on the restricted isometry constant and the mutual coherence of the basis. For piecewise constant functions, we develop conditions utilizing the mutual incoherence framework. Additionally, we propose a novel metric termed "mutual energy," which facilitates the derivation of these criteria in the mutual incoherence format.

The P4 language enables the definition of programmable, reconfigurable packet processors utilizing a match-action table framework. Although the original P14 specification did not explicitly address these tables, the community-driven P4.14 update formalized them, introducing a new compiler phase to translate high-level logic into low-level implementation details. This paper introduces an open-source P14 compiler back-end designed for the Extensible Packet Processing Unit (eXPPU), a research platform supporting programmable logic. By mapping P14 match-action tables directly to eXPPU table units, this system allows for the deployment of large-scale tables that surpass the limitations of conventional fixed-function hardware.

This study examines the discretization of the vector transport equation using the lowest-order Raviart-Thomas finite element method on quadrilateral meshes. We evaluate four distinct approaches for handling vector transport within the element interiors: two standard techniques, one newly proposed method, and one existing method adapted from previous research. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the two standard schemes yield second-order accuracy, whereas both the new proposal and the adapted alternative achieve third-order accuracy.

Federated learning (FL) has emerged as a promising privacy-preserving framework for distributed machine learning, yet it is not immune to privacy breaches. Recent studies have demonstrated that FL servers can reconstruct private data from model updates, prompting the FL community to adopt differential privacy (DP) as a rigorous standard for protecting user information. This paper investigates the tension between FL model accuracy, fairness, and privacy. We begin by establishing a formal definition of fairness within the FL context and demonstrate that, even when employing DP-secured federated averaging (DP-SGD), FL systems can perpetuate biased outcomes. Specifically, we prove that the bias inherent in local datasets transfers to the global model, with the magnitude of this bias contingent upon the specific aggregation strategy used. Consequently, we propose a novel aggregation method designed to mitigate bias in FL. Empirical evaluations across MNIST and FEMNIST datasets confirm that our approach significantly reduces bias while maintaining robust model utility.

The LHCb collaboration reports the observation of an excited $B_c^+$ state, denoted as $B_c(2S)^+$, through the decay channel $B_c(2S)^+ \to B^+ \pi^+ \pi^-$. This observation stems from an analysis of $3.0\,\text{fb}^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data collected at center-of-mass energies of 7 and 8 TeV by the LHCb experiment. The analysis targets the $B^+ \pi^+ \pi^-$ mass spectrum, utilizing the $B^+ \to K^-\pi^+\pi^+$ decay to isolate the $B_c(2S)^+ \to B^+ \pi^+ \pi^-$ signal. The resulting $B^+ \pi^+ \pi^-$ mass spectrum reveals a clear peak at approximately $6.88\,\text{GeV}/c^2$, corresponding to the $B_c(2S)^+$. The measured mass and width are $6.879 \pm 0.034\,\text{(stat)} \pm 0.015\,\text{(syst)}\,\text{GeV}/c^2$ and $10.4 \pm 1.4\,\text{(stat)} \pm 1.0\,\text{(syst)}\,\text

This paper introduces a novel family of Runge-Kutta methods designed for solving differential equations, where the method order corresponds to the stage count. These are termed continuous-Phase Runge-Kutta methods because their Butcher tableau entries are defined by solutions to specific polynomial differential equations. The article establishes the existence and uniqueness of these Butcher tableaus, proves the optimality of Gaussian variants, and provides a means to generate $s$-stage Runge-Kutta methods of order $s+1$ for any $s \geq 1$.

The advancement of deep neural networks relies heavily on the availability of massive datasets and the computational power of large-scale hardware. To effectively utilize extensive resources, researchers have developed various model-parallel strategies, which, however, introduce significant communication overhead that can become a performance bottleneck. This study introduces a novel model-parallel training approach designed to mitigate these communication costs. The core mechanism involves partitioning the network into multiple regions, where each region is assigned to a distinct computing node. This method ensures that communication remains localized, thereby reducing the total volume of data exchanged. Furthermore, the system employs a synchronization protocol to align the network's regions, guaranteeing consistent inference outcomes. Experimental results demonstrate that this technique substantially lowers communication overhead, achieving a performance improvement of up to 2.5 times.

This study examines the dissipation-induced dynamics of a three-dimensional time-dependent Hénon-Heiles system, specifically analyzing the evolution of its basin boundaries through the lens of Wada topology. We demonstrate that the system's chaotic attractor arises from a folded invariant torus, which is sustained by a balance between energy loss and a feeble pumping mechanism. Furthermore, we show that the coexistence of boundary-fractal Wada points across three distinct basins results from the intersection of two invariant tori. Our findings indicate that the presence of minimal dissipation not only stabilizes the chaotic attractor but also actively drives and intensifies the Wada fractal structure at the basin boundaries.

We introduce a new light boson that modifies the flavor perception of food and beverages, hypothesized to exist within the framework of the "taste-changing force" proposed by the Japanese particle physicist Taro Suzuki. This novel entity is characterized by a coupling to the nuclear mass and a distinct coupling to quark mixing, which governs its impact on sensory experience. Our analysis reveals that this boson could persist for an unexpectedly long duration, spanning from $10^4$ to $10^6$ seconds, contingent upon its influence on taste. Furthermore, we outline future experimental strategies designed to detect this particle.

Human action recognition in videos is a challenging task that demands the ability to filter out irrelevant visual information. To address this, we introduce a Hierarchical Focus Network designed to identify key features across multiple temporal and spatial scales. The model employs two distinct attention modules: the first operates on the frame level to select significant frames, while the second analyzes the content within those frames to highlight important regions. Experiments conducted on two prominent datasets, HMDB51 and UCF101, demonstrate that this approach surpasses current state-of-the-art methods.

This study investigates the thermodynamic properties of Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter (RNdS) black holes interacting with a scalar field, specifically analyzing the equation of state for both canonical and grand canonical ensembles. We further examine the validity of the weak (feeble) cosmic censorship hypothesis under varying conditions of temperature and scalar coupling. Our findings indicate that the black hole reaches its extremal state when temperature approaches zero, thereby upholding the weak cosmic censorship hypothesis. Additionally, we observe that the specific heat exhibits a singularity at the critical point of the second-order phase transition, a characteristic shared by both ensembles.

This study examines the emergence of stars within a simplified model of a protoplanetary disk, where a central star is surrounded by a rotating gaseous disk and a population of planetesimals. The model incorporates the formation of dust grains from planetesimals, their subsequent growth into larger bodies, and the central star's radiation pressure acting on dust. The system is modeled using a set of coupled partial differential equations, which are solved numerically. The results indicate that the system naturally evolves toward a stable, starlit equilibrium state. The study also analyzes the system's behavior under various conditions, including changes in the initial mass of the planetesimals and the magnitude of radiation pressure.

We introduce a straightforward method for estimating the entropy of any probability distribution using nested sampling. This technique is applicable to both continuous and discrete systems and functions effectively across high-dimensional spaces. We demonstrate the utility of this approach by calculating the entropies of discrete and continuous distributions, as well as determining the entropies of ensembles within statistical mechanics.

This study examines a nonlinear hyperbolic conservation law featuring a discontinuous flux function, with particular focus on the role of entropy conditions in defining unique solutions. The authors introduce two categories of entropy-adapted solutions: those utilizing $\mathcal{M}_f(\mathbb{R})$-valued measures and those based on $\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{R}^2)$-valued measures. The latter class encompasses both standard and "fragile" solutions, the distinction arising from how they treat the entropy deficit across discontinuities in the solution. The paper demonstrates that, for a specific subset of entropy conditions, fragile solutions yield non-uniqueness. Furthermore, the authors establish a robust framework for the numerical approximation of these $\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{R}^2)$-valued measure solutions.

The escalating volume of network assaults necessitates the development of intrusion detection systems (IDS) capable of identifying and countering attacks. While machine learning (ML) has emerged as a primary method for detecting attacks, many existing models are too resource-intensive for use on devices with limited capabilities. This paper introduces NBcoded, a novel ML-based IDS designed specifically for resource-constrained environments. The framework leverages a Naive Bayes classifier and an encoding technique to transform raw network traffic into a format suitable for NB analysis. The proposed approach was evaluated using the NSL-KDD dataset, demonstrating superior performance compared to several current methods, achieving an accuracy of 99.99%, a Kappa score of 99.99%, and an F1 score of 99.99%.

This paper investigates the solvable characteristics of activity sets, denoted as $G^x = \{g(x) \mid g \in G\}$, where $G$ represents a group acting on a space $X$. We demonstrate that if $G$ is a solvable group, then its activity set $G^x$ forms a solvable subgroup within the general symmetric group $\mathrm{Sym}(X)$ whenever $|X|$ is finite. Furthermore, we establish the converse: for any solvable subgroup $H$ of $\mathrm{Sym}(X)$, there exists a solvable group $G$ such that $G^x = H$. Additionally, these findings extend to cases where $X$ is countably infinite, provided an appropriate definition of solvability is applied to $G$.

Movement is a fundamental biological trait, essential for functions ranging from cellular division to animal foraging. While researchers have extensively studied how motion influences physiology and behavior, the specific nature of these movements remains poorly understood. This study introduces a computational technique designed to identify biological motion within video footage. The method relies on a generative model that characterizes motion through a set of trajectories, utilizing a Bayesian framework to infer these paths from pixel data. The proposed algorithm is validated using both simulated data and real-world video recordings of various cell types. Furthermore, the system is applied to analyze the dynamics of migrating cells, demonstrating its utility in quantifying biological movement.

We introduce a quantum algorithm designed to accelerate H\"older's inequality, a technique frequently utilized within network flow frameworks. This approach achieves a speedup of $\tilde{O}(m^{1/2}n^{1/4})$ compared to the fastest existing classical method, which operates in $O(mn)$ time.

We introduce a methodology for uncovering physical laws from observational data, which relies on the premise that physical systems adhere to global constraints. This approach contrasts with standard techniques that focus solely on local data properties, such as derivatives or probability distributions. Our proposed framework is versatile, capable of identifying both differential and integral equations, and we demonstrate its utility through various applications.

This study presents a search for long-lived charged particles with substantial ionisation energy loss conducted by the ATLAS detector at the LHC, utilizing the complete Run 2 dataset ($36~\text{fb}^{-1}$) from $pp$ collisions at $\sqrt{s} = 13~\text{TeV}$. The analysis targets long-lived particles that decay within the detector volume, manifesting as tracks with high specific ionisation ($dE/dx$) and significant time-of-flight delays. The results are interpreted within the framework of the decay of a heavy neutral boson ($Z'$) into a pair of long-lived charged particles. The analysis finds no evidence for such a signal, establishing exclusion limits at 95% confidence level for $Z'$ boson masses exceeding $1.5~\text{TeV}$ (assuming a branching ratio of 100% into $\tilde{\chi}_1^\pm \tilde{\chi}_1^\pm$) and $1.6~\text{TeV}$ (assuming a branching ratio of 100% into $\tilde{\tilde{t}} \tilde{\tilde{t}}$).

We introduce an integrated quantum light source based on a ridge semiconductor microcavity that emits single photons with near-unity performance. By leveraging the microcavity's inherent Purcell enhancement, we achieve a high on-off ratio of 99.9% and a maximum second-order correlation suppression of 0.0003. Furthermore, our source delivers a record-breaking figure of merit of 0.9997, indicating exceptional single-photon purity and yield. These results establish a new benchmark for integrated quantum photonic technologies.

The boson summit, representing a peak in the static structure factor $S(0)$, is a distinctive feature found in various disordered systems. In this work, we examine the boson summit within the context of randomly occupied square lattices using neutron scattering techniques. Our findings reveal that the summit's visibility hinges on the scattering length distribution among the scatterers. We further analyze the summit in terms of the system's ground state and its connection to the four-point susceptibility.

In high-precision physics, the theoretical framework for particle interactions is established by the Standard Model, with its predictions derived from perturbative expansions of scattering amplitudes. These expansions rely on Feynman integrals, which are evaluated using multi-scale and multi-loop techniques. This paper examines the computational strategies employed for such complex integrals, with a specific focus on the differential equation method and the application of generalized polylogarithms.

We introduce a framework to analyze the absorption of scattered light by resonant nanostructures. This approach centers on energy absorption eigenchannels, which are defined as the modes responsible for the maximum absorption at a specific wavelength. We demonstrate that the total absorption across all wavelengths can be expressed as a sum rule, linking it to the average number of eigenchannels activated at each wavelength. Furthermore, we establish an analogous sum rule for the average count of these eigenchannels at a given wavelength, which correlates with the average number of open scattering channels.

The 3-kpc Arm, a newly identified galactic structure, is situated approximately 10° from the Galactic Center and lies roughly 3 kpc away. This arm is defined by a concentration of HII regions, molecular clouds, and young stellar populations. Our analysis of the 2MASS All-Sky Catalogue of Point Sources reveals that the arm's stellar component is primarily composed of stars with ages between 100 and 300 million years and masses ranging from 1 to 3 solar masses. These stars are arranged in a spiral configuration that extends from the Galactic Center out to the galactic edge, with a pitch angle of roughly 20°. The arm's leading edge is marked by the NGC 346 starburst cluster, which is located about 10° from the center. Additionally, the arm exhibits a distinct break at a Galactocentric radius of roughly 15°, likely caused by the gravitational influence of the Sagittarius (Sgr) Dwarf Galaxy. Multi-objective optimization seeks a set of Pareto-optimal outcomes, yet recent research indicates that incorporating a third objective can yield solutions exhibiting significant phenotypic diversity. This paper investigates the nature of such multi-phenotypic Pareto sets, specifically examining their stability under minor objective function perturbations and their resistance to the addition of supplementary objectives. We introduce a novel metric for quantifying solution diversity and employ it to analyze various multi-solution optimization scenarios. Our findings reveal that while the presence of diversity is not guaranteed, the resulting Pareto sets demonstrate robustness against both perturbations and new objectives. Furthermore, we explore the interplay between solution diversity and algorithmic performance, noting that although evolutionary algorithms struggle to fully exploit these diverse solutions, they remain capable of locating the Pareto set.

This study introduces the three-dimensional (3D) steady roommates problem (3D-SRP), a novel extension of the classic roommates problem to three spatial dimensions. In this model, agents occupy points within a 3D Euclidean space and hold preferences over their locations based on additive utility derived from the Euclidean distance. We define the 3D-SRP as finding a partition of the agent set into pairs, where each pair shares a common preferred point, and every agent prefers their assigned meeting point over any unoccupied alternative.

Our research establishes that the problem remains NP-hard even in the two-dimensional (2D) Euclidean setting. Furthermore, we present a pseudo-polynomial time algorithm for solving the 2D case.

This study examines the impact of distinct electron-phonon interaction mechanisms on valley physics within two-dimensional materials. We analyze the renormalization of valley Zeeman splitting and the valley Hall effect, driven by both deformation potential and piezoelectric coupling. Our findings indicate that electron-phonon coupling significantly alters valley Zeeman splitting, a modification that is highly sensitive to the valley-specific nature of lattice vibrations. Conversely, the contribution of these same mechanisms to the valley Hall effect is found to be negligible.

This work investigates the Gromov-Hoffman structure of metric clouds within a fixed dimension $d$. We demonstrate that the space of $d$-dimensional metric clouds, equipped with the Gromov-Hausdorff distance, forms a complete metric space. Additionally, we establish the existence of a "metric cloud hub" for every finite cloud in this space.

This paper introduces a millimeter-wave patch antenna featuring a bandwidth of 30% and an expansive spatial coverage. The design utilizes a dual-layer configuration where the top layer incorporates a split-ring resonator (SRR) positioned above the standard patch. This SRR is tuned to a specific frequency to create a narrow band-stop filter, resulting in a broad passband. Simultaneously, the SRR's geometry is optimized to enhance the antenna's radiation pattern in the -30 dB direction. Simulation results for the 5G band (24–28 GHz) confirm a measured bandwidth of 30%, spanning from 24 GHz to 31.2 GHz. Furthermore, the -30 dB spatial range extends from 0° to ±80°, with a peak gain of 5.2 dBi.

Although fault-tolerant quantum computing is essential for practical quantum applications, current hardware remains highly susceptible to errors. We introduce a machine learning framework designed to build fault-resilient quantum circuits by integrating reinforcement learning with a neural network-based coding strategy. This approach trains a policy to select optimal stabilizer codes for every gate within a circuit, guided by a reward mechanism that favors minimal overhead alongside high fault resistance. By leveraging a recurrent neural network to approximate this policy, we achieve rapid, near-optimal code selection. Our simulations on superconducting qubit architectures demonstrate that these learned strategies outperform existing methods in both fault resilience and resource efficiency.

We introduce an optical quantum-light-leaping cavity framework designed to achieve ultra-precise measurements of phase shifts. By integrating two optical resonators, the proposed system utilizes the dynamics of double-resonator quantum leaps to surpass the standard quantum limit, reaching Heisenberg-level precision. The study examines the trade-off between measurement fidelity and the frequency of cavity quantum leaps, demonstrating that the leap-based metrological advantage persists even when fidelity is high. Furthermore, the protocol is robust against losses within the cavities and detection inefficiencies.

This study examines direct photon-hadron correlations in Au+Au and d+Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{_{NN}}}=200$ MeV, utilizing data from the PHENIX experiment. The correlated yields are measured as a function of the jet transverse momentum ($p_{_{T}}$) and the pseudorapidity gap ($\Delta\eta$) across various centrality bins. The observed suppression of hadrons within the jet cone and the corresponding modification of the direct photon spectrum in Au+Au collisions are analyzed alongside d+Au results to isolate medium effects on jet fragmentation. Furthermore, the enhanced direct photon spectrum in Au+Au collisions is interpreted as evidence of jet fragmentation modifications, while the excess of correlated photons at large $\Delta\eta$ is attributed to the underlying event. These findings are contrasted with predictions from Monte Carlo simulations.

We introduce a digital–analog hybrid approach utilizing quantum computers to simulate fermionic systems. This method recasts fermionic creation and annihilation operators as sequences of single-qubit Hamiltonians acting upon a string of qubits representing fermionic modes. By leveraging the Lefshetz–Jordan–Wieland (LJW) transformation, we map these operators to nearest- and next-nearest-neighbor interactions within a quantum register. Analog evolution under these Hamiltonians is interleaved with discrete digital quantum gates, enabling the construction of general fermionic many-body Hamiltonians. We demonstrate the validity of this protocol by emulating the one-dimensional Hubbard model and the Kane–Meblel effect, showcasing its capacity to handle complex many-body physics.

Although deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved remarkable success in numerous tasks, their tendency to overfit remains a significant hurdle. To address this, researchers have explored various regularization strategies, including weight decay, dropout, and label smoothing. However, these methods often lack a solid theoretical basis and may even degrade performance in specific scenarios. This paper introduces a novel regularization technique, termed Feature Dropout, which aims to mitigate overfitting by randomly deactivating features within the final layer. We establish a theoretical framework demonstrating that Feature Dropout functions as an implicit regularizer by establishing a link between it and the excess risk of the DNN. Furthermore, we prove that this approach yields superior generalization compared to standard weight decay. Empirical results across multiple image classification benchmarks confirm that Feature Dropout not only enhances generalization but also surpasses existing state-of-the-art regularization methods.

Three-dimensional (3D) laser scanning microscopy (LSM) is a widely adopted technique for deep-tissue imaging, yet its efficacy is hindered by the heterogeneous optical properties of biological samples. To overcome this limitation, integrating LSM with spatial light modulators (SLM) offers a promising solution for beam shaping, allowing for the simultaneous generation of multiple complex wavefronts to create various focal points. This study introduces an iterative algorithm based on a fuzzy logic controller (FLC) for designing FLC-SLM systems. The proposed FLC-SLM framework enables the concurrent formation of several distinct 3D structures within the volume. Simulation results demonstrate that the FLC-SLM approach achieves superior performance in generating multiple 3D shapes compared to both the conventional Gaussian beam method and the genetic algorithm-based SLM strategy.
